introduction: The guide opens with a duty laid on everyone: “Teach ye the Cause of God”, the most meritorious of deeds, acceptable only from one who firmly believes. The readings then say how it is to be done. One soul guided is worth more than the earth’s riches; speech must be wise, kindly and fitted to the hearer; deeds weigh more than words; some seasons call for concealment; help comes to those who arise; and the work is carried by classes, by travel and by particular lives. Mission is an old subject, and its classic texts stand beside the readings here: the charge at the end of Matthew, Paul’s “woe is unto me, if I preach not”, the Qur’an’s “call with wisdom and fair exhortation”, a hadith on red camels, Confucius on when to speak and when to keep silent. So do those who doubt the whole enterprise. The Gospel has a woe for those who cross sea and land to make one proselyte, Thoreau would run from anyone coming to do him good, Mencius thinks the trouble with people is that they like to teach, Vivekananda asks that no one be converted, and Locke marks where persuading ends and compelling begins. The readings are best understood as an answer to both companies.
questions: The readings make teaching everyone’s duty; the Gospel condemns those who “compass sea and land to make one proselyte”, and Thoreau would run from a benefactor. What in the readings distinguishes the teaching they ask for from what these voices fear?

“Speak to each soul according to their capacity.” Compare Paul’s milk and meat, Confucius on the one corner, and Paul’s refusal to please men. Where does adapting to a hearer end and altering the message begin?

Several readings counsel concealment and others unceasing proclamation; the Gospel asks for the wisdom of serpents and for preaching on the housetops, and Daniel opens his windows. How might a community decide which its circumstances call for?
Deeds, the readings say, exert greater influence than words. What do Chaucer’s Parson, Portia and Whitman each add, and why is a warning against goodness done to be seen needed beside them?
The teacher is told not to look to acceptance or rejection, and the Qur’an says that God guides whom He will. What, then, is a teacher responsible for, and what not?
Mencius says the evil of men is that they like to be teachers of others. Which readings on the teacher’s heart, on ordeals and on becoming a learner first, speak to that danger?

outside.why: “God hath prescribed unto every one the duty of proclaiming His Message.” The Gospel of Matthew ends with the same charge, given to eleven men on a mountain: go and teach all nations.
The reading makes teaching a duty laid on every believer and the most meritorious of deeds. Paul feels it as necessity and claims no merit for it: woe to him if he does not preach.

Teaching is acceptable, the reading says, “only when he that teacheth the Cause is already a firm believer”. The Gospel has a harder word for zeal that crosses sea and land to make one convert and leaves him worse than it found him. What separates the teaching the reading asks for from proselytizing?
“Arise for the triumph of My cause.” Isaiah overheard the question that goes with such a summons, who will go, and gave the answer in four words.

“The most important of all things is the guidance of the nations and peoples of the world.” Paul reasons his way to the same priority by a chain of questions: how shall they believe in one of whom they have not heard?
“Unloose your tongues, and proclaim unceasingly His Cause.” Peter and John, forbidden to speak by a court, replied that they could not but speak what they had seen and heard.
“In the skies of this world be dazzling stars.” Daniel promises that brightness to one kind of person in particular: those who turn many to righteousness.

“Whoso quickeneth but a single soul in this Revelation, it is as though he had quickened all humanity.” The form of the saying is the Qur’an’s, which says it of saving a life, and the Qur’an gives it as an older decree to the Children of Israel.
All are to teach “to the extent of their ability”. A saying of Muḥammad sets the same low threshold: convey, even if it is a single sentence.

The reading lays the duty of teaching on everyone. Locke grants every person the same commission, to exhort and convince by reasoning, and draws its limit at once: to compel belongs to no private person, and in religion not even to the magistrate. What keeps persuasion from becoming pressure?

“At all times have We enjoined upon the servants of God that which is right, and forbidden them that which is wrong.” The Qur’an asks for a community that does this: inviting to goodness, enjoining right conduct.
“Deliver to mankind this joyous message … bring to men’s ears these happy tidings.” Isaiah sees the messenger from a distance, on the mountains, and calls his feet beautiful.
“Rest not, by day or night; seek ye no moment’s peace.” The charge to Timothy has the same urgency: be instant in season and out of season.

The reading looks to the day when “the whole earth” is enveloped in the light of one Revelation. Vivekananda told the Parliament of Religions that no one should become a convert to another faith: each must assimilate the others and grow by its own law. Is the reading’s hope the one he opposed?

“Deliver the Message with an eloquent tongue.” Laozi distrusts the ready speaker: the one who knows does not care to speak. When is eloquence a service to a truth and when a sign that it has not been understood?

“Limit thy thoughts to teaching the Faith.” Thoreau describes how such single-mindedness can look from the other side: if he knew a man was coming with the conscious design of doing him good, he would run for his life. What must a teacher be for the taught not to run?
“Even as the clouds let us shed down tears”, and think day and night of spreading the fragrances. The psalmist’s sower also goes out weeping and comes back with sheaves.
“It is better to guide one soul than to possess all that is on earth.” The shepherd of the parable leaves ninety-nine sheep for one, and heaven is said to rejoice over that one.
The guide and the guided, says the reading, “will both be recipients of God’s tender mercy”. The Letter of James promises the same double benefit: a soul saved, and a multitude of sins covered.

The reading speaks of one person guiding another. The Qur’an tells its own Prophet that he does not guide those he loves; God guides whom He will. What, then, is the part of the one who is said to guide?
All are servants of one God who created and provides for all, the reading says; “therefore, why should men be unjust and unkind to each other?” Malachi asks the same question from the same premise.
“Then will aggression crumble away … and the structure of oneness be raised.” Micah’s picture of that day has swords beaten into ploughshares and each household unafraid under its vine and fig tree.
The reading quotes a saying to ʿAlī: “If God guide, through thee, one soul, it is better for thee than all the riches!” This is the saying as al-Bukhārī records it, where the riches are red camels.
“These are the days of seed sowing.” The Preacher’s advice to the sower is to keep at it morning and evening, since no one knows which sowing will prosper.
“He who sows a seed in this day will behold his reward in the fruits and harvest.” Paul keeps the sower modest: one plants, another waters, and God gives the increase.
“Deeds exert greater influence than words.” Asked what makes a superior man, Confucius gave the order of the two: he acts before he speaks, and then speaks according to his actions.

“If it be Our pleasure We shall render the Cause victorious through the power of a single word.” Isaiah’s God speaks of His word in the same way: like rain, it does not return without doing what it was sent for.

The truth is to be proclaimed “by diffusing the sweet savours of God”. The Letter to the Colossians uses another sense for the same quality in speech: seasoned with salt, and wise toward those outside.
“Proclaim the words of thy Lord unto His servants, that perchance they may shake off their slumber.” The Letter to the Ephesians has the proclamation itself: awake, thou that sleepest.
The wise must summon people “with the utmost kindness and love”. The Qur’an gives the method in a verse the readings in this section echo more than once: call with wisdom and fair exhortation.
The Command is to be conveyed “with wisdom and utterance”, lest clamour be raised. Proverbs prizes the fitting word as a jeweller would: apples of gold in a setting of silver.

“Trust not every claimant … nor reveal that which is hidden to every supplicant.” Confucius names the two mistakes: not to speak to one who can be spoken with wastes the person, and to speak to one who cannot wastes the words.
“Some souls are attracted by one word and repelled by another.” The Sermon on the Mount puts the caution more roughly: do not give what is holy to those who will trample it and turn on the giver.
“One must consider the capacity and receptivity of the people and be moderate in speech.” Paul describes his own practice of meeting hearers where they stood: to the weak he became as weak.

The reading advises moderation before a mixed audience of “all religions and sects”. Paul, in another letter, refuses the suspicion that he trims his message: if he sought to please men he would not be a servant of Christ. When does fitting one’s speech to the hearers become pleasing them?
“One must speak to each soul according to their capacity.” Paul tells the Corinthians that he did so with them: milk, and not meat, because they could not yet bear it.

The reading speaks of bringing souls to maturity by “the hands of training”. Plato denies that teaching puts sight into blind eyes: the power is in the soul already, and the teacher’s work is to turn it toward the light.
“Be gentle to every outsider; suffer from enemies and behave with patience.” The proverb gives the plain mechanics: a soft answer turns away wrath.
The reading asks for justice toward the unjust and faithfulness toward the oppressor. When Moses and Aaron are sent to Pharaoh himself, they are told to speak to him a gentle word.

“Your behavior towards your neighbor should be such as to manifest clearly the signs of the one true God.” Whitman claims the same method for himself and his companions on the road: not arguments, but presence.

Whoever teaches must first be adorned “with the ornament of an upright and praiseworthy character”. Portia knows how rare that is: she could sooner teach twenty what is good than be one of the twenty to follow it.
Without character, the reading says, a teacher “can never” win the receptive. Chaucer praises his country parson for exactly this: first he did, and afterwards he taught.
The teacher’s character must come before his message. The Qur’an asks the believers the question that makes the rule: why say ye that which ye do not?

“Let your light shine before the eyes of men”, the Báb tells his disciples, in the Gospel’s words. The same sermon warns against doing good in order to be seen. How does a character draw others to God without being displayed to them?
“Look not to rejection or acceptance, but rather to the service whereunto ye have been bidden.” The Qur’an relieves its Prophet of the same burden: he is a reminder, not a warder over them.
The teacher is to speak for God’s sake and not count acceptances. The disciples in the Gospel are told what to do when they are refused: shake off the dust and go on.
“When he is enkindled with the fire of His love … his words shall set ablaze those that hear him.” Jeremiah tried to keep silent and found the word a fire shut up in his bones.
“Be not grieved that thou possessest not outward learning and penmanship.” Moses made the same excuse at the burning bush and was asked who made man’s mouth.
“Travel not the way without a guide, nor accept every guide’s words. Many guides are themselves astray.” The Gospel’s warning is the same, with the ditch at the end of it.
One must first “value these ordeals, willingly accept them, and eagerly welcome them; only then should he proceed with teaching”. The apostles left a flogging rejoicing, and went on teaching daily.

The reading observes that teaching stimulates the teacher: his own faith grows as he speaks. Mencius names a danger in the same pleasure: the trouble with people is that they like to be teachers of others. How does a teacher tell the growth the reading means from the liking Mencius means?
“Certainly we shall not deny access to members of other religions.” The Qur’an sets a matching rule for speech about what others worship: do not revile it, lest they revile God in return.

The reading keeps its school open to other religions and yet wants its own character evident, and no “breeding ground for superstitions”. Aśoka’s edict asks for more than access: one should listen to and respect the doctrines of others, since praising only one’s own harms it. Where does the reading draw its line, and why there?

A Russian official “hath become somewhat attracted to the Cause” and may come to believe “little by little”. King Agrippa told Paul he was almost persuaded, and Paul wished him wholly so, except for the chains.
Among the Theosophists the reading advises speaking of what is held in common, the oneness of humanity and concord. Paul began at Athens from an altar he found there, to an unknown God.
“Invite thou the receptive souls unto God’s holy court, that … they may not remain deprived of the heavenly Fountain.” Isaiah’s invitation is to everyone who thirsts.

The reading hopes that “high-ranking and influential persons” will be taught. Paul reminded the Corinthians how few of the wise, mighty or noble were among them, and saw a purpose in it. What is gained when the influential are won, and what did Paul think was shown when they were not?
“Those whom you find receptive to your call, share with them the epistles.” The parable of the sower is about the difference the ground makes to one and the same seed.
The Báb’s instruction is to give more to the receptive. Confucius taught on the same principle: he opened the truth only to the eager, and expected one corner shown to bring back the other three.

“The seeds of wisdom must be deposited in receptive soil”, and the Cause is not to be mentioned to the government. The Gospel sends its messengers out as sheep among wolves, with the same counsel of prudence.
If many “openly and manifestly speak the Word of God among people”, agitation follows, says the reading. The Preacher allows for both seasons: a time to keep silence and a time to speak.

The reading counsels against speaking openly. In the same chapter that asks for the wisdom of serpents, Jesus tells his disciples to preach from the housetops what they heard in the ear. How is a community to know which season it is in?
“Keep hidden from all anyone who accepts the Faith.” The Gospel names one such believer, a disciple “secretly for fear”, and records what he found the courage to do in the end.
The reading arranges for teaching in secret, in a private house. Daniel, when prayer was made a crime, prayed as before with his windows open. Is concealment a lesser faithfulness, or another kind?
The reading hopes the call may reach “the Eskimos” and the farthest islands. Acts begins with the same widening map: Jerusalem, Judaea, Samaria, the uttermost part of the earth.
If they show such magnanimity, “the heavenly cohorts will reinforce them”. Zechariah was given the principle for a small community facing a great task: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
“No capacity is limited when led by the Spirit of God!” Paul says why the vessel is left plain: so that the power may be seen to be God’s and not ours.
“Speak, and the confirmations of the Spirit will come.” The Gospel makes the same promise to those brought before courts: what to say will be given in that hour.

The reading puts the speaking first and the confirmation after. Aesop’s waggoner waits on his knees for help and is told to put his shoulder to the wheel. What does each say about the order of effort and aid?
“Although now ye be learners, the hope is that … ye will become teachers.” The Second Letter to Timothy plans the same succession: commit what you have heard to those who can teach others also.
The hope is that “the instant a question is asked” an answer will be ready. The First Letter of Peter asks for that readiness, and for its manner: with meekness and fear.

The reading wants a class that can answer any question at once. Pope warns the quick learner that shallow draughts intoxicate, and only drinking deeply sobers. What should a class do with a question it cannot yet answer?
“When ye meet each other, convey the glad-tidings and impart hope to one another.” Malachi says of those who spoke often to one another that their conversation was heard and written down.
The reading asks for nights and days spent studying together. The Letter to the Hebrews says what meeting is for: to provoke one another to love and good works.
“The women believers have organized meetings where they will learn how to teach.” Confucius set the rule that such a meeting applies: in teaching there should be no distinction of classes.
“Teaching the children is indispensable and obligatory.” Deuteronomy makes it the business of the whole day, at home and on the road, lying down and rising up.
The teachers are told that they are “educating your spiritual children”. Paul uses the same language of his converts, whom he says he has begotten through the gospel.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says he inhales the fragrance of the love of God “from every meeting place where the Word of God is uttered”. The Gospel’s promise about small gatherings is of a presence too.

The reading hopes the fame of the Cause will be “diffused throughout the East and the West”. Kipling’s ballad begins with the line everyone remembers, that the twain shall never meet, and ends by saying when they do. What kind of meeting does each have in mind?
“All countries, in the estimation of the one true God, are but one country.” Garrison put the same sentence at the head of his newspaper.
“The believers of God must display the utmost effort” throughout those regions. Jesus sent seventy ahead of him two by two, with the remark that the harvest is great and the labourers few.

“Rest thou not for a moment, travel to the North and South of the country.” Mark Twain thought travel changes the traveller first: it is fatal to prejudice. What does the one who goes out to teach have to learn on the way?

The traveller is to say that “Bahá’u’lláh laid the foundation of universal peace fifty years ago”. In 1849 Victor Hugo told a peace congress in Paris that a day would come when the nations of Europe would be one fraternity.
“They shall speak in every tongue, and interpret every hidden meaning.” The pattern is Pentecost, where each hearer heard in his own language.
The reading quotes the Qur’an: “One grain will bring forth seven sheaves.” This is the verse; it speaks there of those who spend in God’s way.
In the lifetime of Christ the firm believers “were few and numbered”, and in a few years countless souls followed. His own figure for that growth is the mustard seed.
“Those states are like unto dead bodies: they must breathe into them the breath of life.” Ezekiel is told to prophesy to the wind over a valley of the slain, and they stand up.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá was warned that Montreal was too fanatical to listen, and went. Jonah expected nothing of Nineveh, and the whole city believed at a sentence.
“The call of praise is raised” by those who arose with firmness. The first herald of the Gospel claimed to be only that, a voice.
The reading honours one “held fast, time and again, in the claws of ravening wolves”, who went on proclaiming. Paul’s own record is a list: beaten, stoned, shipwrecked, in perils of every kind.
“They became a guiding torch to the wanderers.” The Gospel says it to its hearers as a fact about them and a duty: a lit candle belongs on a candlestick.

The women are told to “eradicate war and lay the foundation for peace”. UNESCO’s constitution locates the work where the reading does, in people and not in treaties: the defences of peace are built in the minds of men.

“Our answers have not been utilized for controversy and argument.” Milton thought much arguing a sign of health wherever there is much desire to learn, since opinion in good people is knowledge in the making. What is the difference between the controversy the reading avoids and the arguing Milton welcomes?
“Day and night, individually and collectively you have listened.” Paul takes leave of the elders of Ephesus in the same way, reminding them of three years of warning night and day.
“Through your call every sleeping one was awakened.” Socrates describes himself to his judges as a gadfly sent to rouse a great, sluggish horse; he adds that people caught napping are apt to strike.
The call raised “the negligent … from slumber”. Shelley asked to be such a voice, “the trumpet of a prophecy” to an unawakened earth.

A youth who had been in the presence “guided his family to the truth and imparted the gladsome tidings to a great many”. Philip does the same within a verse of being called, and meets a sceptic with three words.
The prayer asks that nothing hinder the one who prays from remembering and praising God. The psalmist’s request is shorter and comes first in many a daily office: open thou my lips.

The prayer asks for help “to deliver Thy Message, and to proclaim Thy Cause”, unmoved by fear. Moses, sent to Pharaoh, prays for the same things: a mind relieved, a task eased, a knot loosed from the tongue.
The prayer asks to teach so “that the dead may speed out of their sepulchers”. John’s Gospel speaks of an hour, already come, when the dead hear a voice and live.

leftOut.saying: “Preach the Gospel at all times; when necessary, use words.”
leftOut.attributed: Commonly attributed to Francis of Assisi.
leftOut.reason: Wanted beside the readings that put a teacher’s deeds before his words, and left out: it is not in the writings of Francis and no early source has it. Chaucer’s Parson and Analects 2.13 stand there instead.

matthew-great-commission.text: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world

corinthians-woe-if-i-preach-not.text: For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel

matthew-compass-sea-and-land.text: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves

isaiah-here-am-i.text: Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me

romans-how-shall-they-hear.text: How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things

acts-cannot-but-speak.text: But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard

isaiah-beautiful-upon-the-mountains.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth

timothy-in-season-out-of-season.text: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all long suffering and doctrine

psalm-sow-in-tears.text: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him

luke-joy-over-one-sinner.text: What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it … I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance

james-converteth-the-sinner.text: Brethren, if any of you do err from the truth, and one convert him; Let him know, that he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins

ecclesiastes-sow-thy-seed.text: In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good

isaiah-word-not-return-void.text: For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it

colossians-seasoned-with-salt.text: Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time. Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man

proverbs-word-fitly-spoken.text: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver

matthew-pearls-before-swine.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you

corinthians-all-things-to-all-men.text: To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some

galatians-please-men.text: For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ

corinthians-milk-not-meat.text: I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able

proverbs-soft-answer.text: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger

matthew-shake-off-the-dust.text: And whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear your words, when ye depart out of that house or city, shake off the dust of your feet

jeremiah-fire-in-my-bones.text: Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay

exodus-slow-of-speech.text: And Moses said unto the Lord, O my Lord, I am not eloquent, neither heretofore, nor since thou hast spoken unto thy servant: but I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue. And the Lord said unto him, Who hath made man's mouth? or who maketh the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? have not I the Lord? Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say

corinthians-not-many-mighty.text: For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty

acts-almost-thou-persuadest.text: Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian. And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds

acts-unknown-god.text: Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, To The Unknown God. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you

matthew-wise-as-serpents.text: Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves

ecclesiastes-time-to-keep-silence.text: A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak

matthew-upon-the-housetops.text: What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops

john-disciple-secretly.text: And after this Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus

acts-uttermost-part.text: But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth

zechariah-not-by-might.text: Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts

corinthians-earthen-vessels.text: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us

matthew-take-no-thought-how-to-speak.text: But when they deliver you up, take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak. For it is not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaketh in you

timothy-teach-others-also.text: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also

peter-ready-to-give-an-answer.text: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear

malachi-spake-often.text: Then they that feared the Lord spake often one to another: and the Lord hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the Lord, and that thought upon his name

hebrews-not-forsaking-assembling.text: And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another

matthew-two-or-three.text: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them

luke-labourers-are-few.text: After these things the Lord appointed other seventy also, and sent them two and two before his face into every city and place, whither he himself would come. Therefore said he unto them, The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few: pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send forth labourers into his harvest

jonah-nineveh-believed.text: And Jonah began to enter into the city a day's journey, and he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them

corinthians-thrice-beaten.text: Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep; In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren; In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness

acts-three-years-with-tears.text: Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears

john-come-and-see.text: Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. And Nathanael said unto him, Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him, Come and see

psalm-open-thou-my-lips.text: O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise

john-dead-shall-hear.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live

quran-invite-to-goodness.text: And there may spring from you a nation who invite to goodness, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency. Such are they who are successful.

quran-allah-guideth-whom-he-will.text: Lo! thou (O Muhammad) guidest not whom thou lovest, but Allah guideth whom He will. And He is Best Aware of those who walk aright.

quran-gentle-word.text: And speak unto him a gentle word, that peradventure he may heed or fear.

quran-remembrancer.text: Remind them, for thou art but a remembrancer, Thou art not at all a warder over them

quran-say-what-ye-do-not.text: O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not

quran-revile-not.text: Revile not those unto whom they pray beside Allah lest they wrongfully revile Allah through ignorance

quran-seven-ears.text: The likeness of those who spend their wealth in Allah's way is as the likeness of a grain which groweth seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains. Allah giveth increase manifold to whom He will. Allah is All-Embracing, All-Knowing.

hadith-convey-one-sentence.text: Convey (my teachings) to the people even if it were a single sentence
hadith-convey-one-sentence.author: Muḥammad
hadith-convey-one-sentence.caveat: The words in brackets are the translator’s.

hadith-red-camels.text: Go to them patiently and calmly till you enter the land. Then, invite them to Islam, and inform them what is enjoined upon them, for, by Allah, if Allah gives guidance to somebody through you, it is better for you than possessing red camels
hadith-red-camels.author: Muḥammad
hadith-red-camels.caveat: Said to ʿAlī before Khaybar; red camels were the most prized of possessions.

analects-may-be-spoken-with.text: When a man may be spoken with, not to speak to him is to err in reference to the man. When a man may not be spoken with, to speak to him is to err in reference to our words. The wise err neither in regard to their man nor to their words
analects-may-be-spoken-with.author: Confucius

analects-one-corner.text: I do not open up the truth to one who is not eager to get knowledge, nor help out any one who is not anxious to explain himself. When I have presented one corner of a subject to any one, and he cannot from it learn the other three, I do not repeat my lesson
analects-one-corner.author: Confucius

analects-acts-before-he-speaks.text: He acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions
analects-acts-before-he-speaks.author: Confucius

plato-gadfly.text: I am that gadfly which God has given the state and all day long and in all places am always fastening upon you, arousing and persuading and reproaching you
plato-gadfly.author: Plato

shakespeare-good-divine.text: It is a good divine that follows his own instructions: I can easier teach twenty what were good to be done, than be one of the twenty to follow mine own teaching
shakespeare-good-divine.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

mencius-like-to-be-teachers.text: The evil of men is that they like to be teachers of others
mencius-like-to-be-teachers.author: Mencius

whitman-convince-by-our-presence.text: I and mine do not convince by arguments, similes, rhymes, We convince by our presence
whitman-convince-by-our-presence.author: Walt Whitman

chaucer-parson.text: This noble ensample to his sheep he yaf, / That first he wroghte, and afterward he taughte; / Out of the gospel he tho wordes caughte; / And this figure he added eek ther-to, / That if gold ruste, what shal iren do
chaucer-parson.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
chaucer-parson.caveat: In Middle English, from Skeat’s edition: “wroghte” is did, “lewed” unlearned.

locke-commission-to-admonish.text: Every man has commission to admonish, exhort, convince another of error, and, by reasoning, to draw him into truth; but to give laws, receive obedience, and compel with the sword, belongs to none but the magistrate
locke-commission-to-admonish.author: John Locke

pope-little-learning.text: A little learning is a dang'rous thing; / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring: / There shallow draughts intoxicate the brain, / And drinking largely sobers us again
pope-little-learning.author: Alexander Pope
